messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: added HMMs, measurement error, meta-analysis
parts:
I added models and a chapter to the manual on
measurement error and meta-analysis. I followed
the definitions in BDA pretty closely.

I also added HMMs, including a model for simple
supervised parameter estimation and a model for
full Bayesian prediction (aka semi-supervised
training or even unsupervised training). It only
needs the forward part of forward-backward,
unlike EM which needs full forward-backward to compute
summary statistics in the E step. I even coded up
a first-best Viterbi decoder in a generated quantities
block. Now I need to find some examples for testing
and write the manual chapter :-)

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] added HMMs, measurement error, meta-analysis
parts:
On 1/23/13 1:10 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> That's awesome! HMMs in Stan is exciting. I don't suppose you
> hand-coded the gradients too?

Afraid not. I didn't even collect up the sufficient
sufficient stats efficiently (it's a no brainer
for the transitions but the emissions are going to
be relatively sparse, so until we have sparse vectors,
I don't think it's worthwhile).

There are SO many different ways to code up HMMs.
For NLP applications like part-of-speech tagging,
you really need to add start-of-sentence and end-of-sentence
transition probabilities; the model below just takes
a long stream. You can use the same trick I used to code
LDA to break the HMMs into a collection of inputs of varying
lengths -- I just thought it got in the way of the basic idea here.

hmm-fit.stan
------------
data {
int<lower=1> K; // num categories
int<lower=1> V; // num words
int<lower=0> N; // num instances
int<lower=1,upper=V> w[N]; // words
int<lower=1,upper=K> z[N]; // categories
vector<lower=0>[K] alpha; // transit prior
vector<lower=0>[V] beta; // emit prior
}
parameters {
simplex[K] theta[K]; // transit probs
simplex[V] phi[K]; // emit probs
}
model {
for (k in 1:K)
theta[k] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
for (k in 1:K)
phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta);
for (n in 1:N)
w[n] ~ categorical(phi[z[n]]);
for (n in 2:N)
z[n] ~ categorical(theta[z[n-1]]);
}

With my Bayesian hat on, I really wonder if there's
any utility in using an informative prior for the emissions
or even building a hierarchical model for emissions and/or
transitions. One step up it makes sense if you have
different corpus collections (like, say, English collected
from multiple sources, which may have different distributions
of both words and parts of speech).

With unlabeled data inputs u, the forward algorithm
for semi-supervision is this:

hmm-fit-semisup.stan
--------------------
model {
...
// forward algorithm
{
real acc[K];
real gamma[M,K];
for (k in 1:K)
gamma[1,k] <- log(phi[k,u[1]]);
for (m in 2:M) {
for (k in 1:K) {
for (j in 1:K)
acc[j] <- log(theta[j,k]) + log(phi[k,u[m]]);
gamma[m,k] <- log_sum_exp(acc);
}
}
lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(gamma[M]);
}
...

I haven't tested this yet, so there may be bugs. It
does parse :-)

- Bob

messages.author: 6ad178c9bfa534b7
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] added HMMs, measurement error, meta-analysis
parts:
Along the lines of the HMM, I wrote a Kalman filter in Stan.  The code is available here: https://gist.github.com/4700387. It is only the most basic multivariate Kalman filter, i.e. it doesn't allow for missing values (I can't get that to work without crashing), and doesn't transform the time series to do univariate filtering.  

I think it would be nice to have some basic Kalman and HMM functions within Stan, which return either the filtered states or just the log-likelihood of the system.  These can be coded in Stan's modeling language, but they take up enough lines of boilerplate code that it starts getting confusing once the inputs of the DLM or HMM are themselves parameters, or if the DLM / HMM is a component of a larger model. 

I'd be willing to give it a go, since I'm already running DLMs in Stan, but I'd need someone to point me in the right direction.

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] added HMMs, measurement error, meta-analysis
parts:
A function to evaluate a standard Gauss-Linear time series would be great.  E.G., something where you could write:

matrix[N,T] state;
matrix[M,T] obs;
matrix[M,N] obs_mat;
cov_matrix[M] obs_sigma;
matrix[N,N] state_mat;
cov_matrix[N] state_sigma;

obs ~ gauss_linear_timeseries(state,obs_mat,obs_sigma,state_mat,state_sigma);

There are a number of generalizations of this that could be made.  E.G., correlated observation/evolution noise, but this basic form would cover 90% of the use cases people think of.

This has been on my TODO list for a while, but it's unlikely that I'll get there soon myself, so feel free :)

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 6ad178c9bfa534b7
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] added HMMs, measurement error, meta-analysis
parts:
That's what I was thinking, but it doesn't need the latent states as an argument to calculate the likelihood. So there'd be functions like 

 real gauss_linear_timeseries_log(matrix obs, matrix obs_mat, matrix obs_sigma, matrix state_mat, matrix state_sigma)

and another version with a matrix indicating missing values in the observations

 real gauss_linear_timeseries_log(matrix obs, matrix obs_mat, matrix obs_sigma, matrix state_mat, matrix state_sigma, matrix missing)
 
The downside of that those functions is that although the prediction errors and variances of the predicted errors are calculated within the function and potentially interesting to the user, they aren't returned to the user. Perhaps I could have a function that returns the predicted states and their variances in a matrix (like KalmanFil in SsfPack http://www.ssfpack.com/files/SsfEctJ.pdf), and then a function that calculates the likelihood given the matrix returned by kalman_filter.

 matrix kalman_filter(matrix obs, matrix obs_mat, matrix obs_sigma, matrix state_mat, matrix state_sigma)
 real gauss_linear_timeseries_log(matrix K)

Is the best way to get started to look at the code for multi_normal_log?  Another question, can functions take arrays of matrices as arguments?
